intro.why: ML code processes millions of records and billions of parameters. The right algorithm and data structure can turn hours into seconds, and clean object design keeps multi-agent systems manageable.

symbols: upper bound on growth of running time
number of halvings from n down to 1
method resolution order (which class's method runs)

sections.title: Time complexity and Big O
sections.plain: How the running time grows as the data grows.
sections.body:
Time complexity describes how running time grows with input size. ML processes millions of records and models with billions of parameters, so growth rates dominate constant factors. Big O gives the order of growth ("how your code slows down as data grows"); in ML we think in terms of samples $n$ and features $d$ (e.g. a linear model's prediction is $O(d)$ per sample, $O(nd)$ for a dataset).

ClassNameExamples
$O(1)$constantarray random access; insert at the head of a linked list; dict lookup (average)
$O(\log n)$logarithmicbinary search
$O(n)$linearloop through an array; search a linked list
$O(n\log n)$linearithmicquicksort (average), mergesort, heapsort
$O(n^2)$quadraticinsertion, selection, bubble sort; all-pairs similarity
$O(n!)$factorialbrute-force travelling salesman; trying every ordering

Telecom churn pipeline (self-study): $O(1)$ cached prediction lookup by customer ID; $O(\log n)$ threshold search over sorted scores; $O(n)$ scoring every customer; $O(n\log n)$ ranking customers by risk; $O(n^2)$ pairwise customer similarity; $O(n!)$ brute-force feature-order optimisation.

sections.title: Lists and tuples
sections.plain: A list is a growable array of references; a tuple is a fixed one.
sections.body:
ML code mostly uses five structures: list, tuple, dict, NumPy array and DataFrame.

List: dynamic, mutable array; can hold mixed types; stored contiguously as an array of references to objects; indexing is $O(1)$. Measured access times stay flat as size grows (about 25.7, 25.65 and 23.93 ns for 10, 10,000 and 1,000,000 elements).

Tuple: immutable ordered collection; heterogeneous; $O(1)$ indexing; more memory-efficient; read-only, so safe for fixed records (about 31.9, 24.99, 25.50 ns).

sections.title: Dictionaries
sections.plain: Look up a value by key in constant time on average.
sections.body: Dictionary: mutable key → value mapping. Keys must be unique and immutable (hashable). Implemented as a hash table, so lookup, insertion and deletion are $O(1)$ on average (worst case $O(n)$ with many collisions). Measured: about 30.05, 35.59, 39.55 ns for 10, 10k and 1M entries: nearly flat.

sections.title: NumPy arrays and vectorisation
sections.plain: Homogeneous numbers in contiguous memory, processed by compiled loops.
sections.body:
NumPy ndarray: mutable, homogeneous (one dtype), multidimensional, stored contiguously, supports vectorised operations; $O(1)$ indexing (about 59.5, 61.2, 62.3 ns: slightly slower for single-element access because a NumPy scalar object is created).

Vectorisation: sum(list) of a million numbers took about 1.943 ms vs np.sum(array) about 0.016 ms: roughly 100× faster, because the loop runs in compiled C over typed memory instead of the interpreter. In ex1 (a different machine): for-loop 23.6 ms, built-in sum 4.2 ms, np.sum 0.31 ms.

sections.title: pandas DataFrames
sections.plain: A labelled 2-D table built on NumPy, with mixed column types.
sections.body: DataFrame: built on NumPy; a two-dimensional labelled table whose columns can have different types; tools for cleaning, filtering, sorting, grouping and handling missing values. Construct from a dict of columns, from a NumPy array with column names, or from a dataset such as Iris (pd.DataFrame(iris.data, columns=iris.feature_names)).

sections.title: Choosing the right data structure
sections.plain: Match the structure to the job: collection, record, lookup, maths or table.
sections.body:
StructureUse forML examples
listDynamic collectionsFeature names, labels, file paths
dictFast lookupFeature → index map, hyperparameters, label encoding
tupleFixed dataShape (rows, cols), image size (224, 224, 3)
NumPy arrayNumerical computationX, y, model weights
DataFrameTabular dataCustomer records, sales, CSV files

Quiz pattern: load a CSV → DataFrame; clean it → DataFrame; feature names → list; name → index map → dict; training data → NumPy array; shape or image dimensions → tuple. A single Iris demo can use all five together.

sections.title: Classes, inheritance and polymorphism
sections.plain: Blueprints, specialisation, and one call that behaves differently by type.
sections.body:
A class is a blueprint with properties and methods (Dog: name, colour, eye colour, height, length; getName()…); an object is an instance (Tommy: green, brown eyes, 17 in tall, 35 in long).

Inheritance enables code reuse. Types: single (B from A), multilevel (C from B from A), hierarchical (B and C from A), multiple (C from A and B), hybrid (a combination).

Polymorphism: compile-time (operator or function overloading) vs run-time (virtual functions, method overriding: the subclass's version runs).

sections.title: OOP for agentic AI, and functional parts
sections.plain: Agents are objects; a multi-agent system is composition.
sections.body:
OOP conceptIn agentic AI
ClassAgent definition
ObjectRunning agent with its own state and memory
InheritanceSpecialised agents from a base Agent
Polymorphismexecute() differs by agent role
EncapsulationMemory, goals and logic kept inside the agent
AbstractionReasoning, planning and tool calls behind simple methods
CompositionA multi-agent system built from agents

Example: a base Agent (client, model, ask_llm(), abstract execute(paper)); ValidationAgent and SummaryAgent override execute (VALID/INVALID; a ~300-word summary); ResearchPaperWorkflow has both and loops for agent in agents: agent.execute(paper). Functional parts stay as standalone functions: read_paper() extracts text, save_result() writes the summary.

Travel example: a FlightInfoAgent (live flight details) and an ItineraryAgent (sightseeing plan) composed in a TravelWorkflow with typed input and result objects, using an agents SDK's Agent, Runner, run configuration and model settings (including reasoning effort). Code example ex2 implements the research-paper version offline.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Big O hides constants: an $O(n)$ Python loop can lose to an $O(n\log n)$ NumPy sort for realistic n.
  • Average vs worst case: quicksort is $O(n^2)$ worst case; dicts degrade with adversarial hashes.
  • x in list is O(n); use a set or dict for membership tests in loops.
  • Composition over inheritance: deep hierarchies are brittle; prefer small agents composed into workflows.

code.title: Complexity in practice: search, lookup and vectorisation
code.explain: Counts binary-search steps (log₂ n), times list scan vs binary search vs dict lookup as n grows, compares loop/sum/np.sum, and shows O(1) indexing for list, tuple, dict and ndarray.
mistakes: Membership tests on lists inside loops.
code.notes: Exact timings vary by machine; the growth pattern is what matters.
code.code:
"""How running time grows: linear vs binary search vs dict lookup, and list vs NumPy.

We count operations (deterministic) and time real calls for growing n, then
compare summing with a Python loop/built-in against NumPy's vectorised sum.
"""
import bisect, math, timeit
import numpy as np

print(f"{'n':>12} {'linear ops':>12} {'binary ops':>11} {'log2 n':>7}")
for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 1_000_000_000]:
    target = n - 1                                # worst case for linear search
    lo, hi, steps = 0, n - 1, 0                   # binary search on 0..n-1, counting halvings
    while lo <= hi:
        steps += 1; mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if mid == target: break
        lo, hi = (mid + 1, hi) if mid < target else (lo, mid - 1)
    print(f"{n:>12,} {n:>12,} {steps:>11} {math.log2(n):7.1f}")

print("\nmeasured lookup time per query (microseconds):")
for n in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]:
    data = list(range(n)); s = set(data); d = {k: k for k in data}; q = n - 1
    lin = timeit.timeit(lambda: q in data, number=20) / 20 * 1e6
    bis = timeit.timeit(lambda: bisect.bisect_left(data, q), number=20000) / 20000 * 1e6
    dic = timeit.timeit(lambda: d[q], number=20000) / 20000 * 1e6
    print(f"  n={n:>9,}: list scan O(n) {lin:9.1f} | binary search O(log n) {bis:5.2f} | dict O(1) {dic:5.2f}")

print("\nsum of 1,000,000 numbers:")
xs = list(range(1_000_000)); arr = np.arange(1_000_000)
def loop_sum():
    t = 0
    for v in xs: t += v
    return t
for name, f in [("Python for-loop", loop_sum), ("built-in sum(list)", lambda: sum(xs)), ("np.sum(array)", lambda: np.sum(arr))]:
    t = min(timeit.repeat(f, number=5, repeat=3)) / 5 * 1000
    print(f"  {name:<20} {t:8.3f} ms")

print("\nindexing is O(1) for all of these (time does not grow with size):")
for n in [10, 10_000, 1_000_000]:
    L = list(range(n)); T = tuple(L); D = dict.fromkeys(L, 0); A = np.arange(n); i = n // 2
    row = [timeit.timeit(lambda: c[i], number=200_000) / 200_000 * 1e9 for c in (L, T, D, A)]
    print(f"  n={n:>9,}: list {row[0]:5.1f} ns  tuple {row[1]:5.1f} ns  dict {row[2]:5.1f} ns  ndarray {row[3]:5.1f} ns")
